hints: Look at the two big trends for Group 17, how oxidising power of the halogens and reducing power of the halides change down the group.
Recall the silver halide colours, white for $\text{AgCl}$, cream for $\text{AgBr}$, yellow for $\text{AgI}$, and remember that gaining electrons makes an anion, not a cation.
Ask yourself if a halogen lower down the group can ever oxidise a halide ion above it, then check which statement fits that rule.
walkthrough:
**Recall the silver nitrate test**

Halide ions give different coloured precipitates with $\text{Ag}^+$. This is a key identification test to remember.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{X}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgX}(s)$$

**Recall halogen oxidising strength**

Oxidising power of the halogens decreases down Group 17. So $\text{F}_2$ is strongest and $\text{I}_2$ is weakest.

$$\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$$

**Recall halide reducing strength**

It is the opposite trend. Reducing power of halide ions increases down the group because larger ions lose electrons more easily.

$$\text{I}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{F}^-$$

**Apply to displacement**

A more powerful halogen can oxidise (take electrons from) a less powerful halide, but not the other way round. So bromine, below chlorine, cannot oxidise chloride ions to chlorine.

options.A: Incorrect. Bromide gives a cream or pale yellow precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$, not white. The white precipitate is $\text{AgCl}$ formed from chloride ions.
options.B: Correct. Bromine ($\text{Br}_2$) is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine ($\text{Cl}_2$), so it cannot remove electrons from $\text{Cl}^-$ to form $\text{Cl}_2$. No reaction occurs when bromine is added to sodium chloride solution.
options.C: Incorrect. Accepting electrons forms a negative ion, an anion ($\text{F} + e^- \rightarrow \text{F}^-$), not a cation. Fluorine is very electronegative and always forms $\text{F}^-$.
options.D: Incorrect. It reverses the trend. Iodide ions are the strongest reducing agents because the large $\text{I}^-$ ion loses electrons most easily. Chloride ions are much weaker reducing agents.
